etymology: Hebrew 'Adorayim, likely “two mounds” or “double honour,” a fortified town in the hill country of Judah, west of Hebron.
biblical_def: Adoraim was one of the cities of defence that Rehoboam built to guard the southern kingdom after the ten tribes tore away: “And Adoraim, and Lachish, and Azekah” (2Ch 11:9). The Chronicler frames the whole enterprise in a single sentence of quiet dignity: “And Rehoboam dwelt in Jerusalem, and built cities for defence in Judah” (2Ch 11:5). Adoraim stood among these strong holds, and the king “fortified the strong holds, and put captains in them, and store of victual, and of oil and wine” (2Ch 11:11). Here is a town of walls and watchmen, of gates barred against the Egyptian and the Edomite. Yet the Reformed reader must set every rampart under the word that governs them all: “Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1). Rehoboam was right to build; Scripture never despises the ordinary means of prudence and defence. But the fortress that trusts its own thickness has already fallen in heart. Adoraim reminds us that the labour of the hand and the keeping of the LORD are not rivals but a covenant: we build the wall, and He alone makes it stand. The believer garrisons his soul with watchfulness and prayer, and rests the outcome wholly upon God.
webster_summary: A fortified city of Judah built by Rehoboam for the kingdom’s defence (2Ch 11:9), witnessing that walls avail nothing except the LORD keep the city.

corruption_summary: A defensive city of Rehoboam; the entry recovers the doctrine that all lawful means of safety rest under the sole keeping of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Adoraim is a name of stone and mortar, and it raises no modern quarrel of its own. Its danger is the oldest one in the heart of man: to build a wall and then to trust the wall. The store of victual and the captains in the gate were good gifts of prudence, and Scripture commends the diligent who look to their defences; folly is not made wise by calling itself faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ordinary means and the sovereign keeping of God are joined, not opposed. Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain (Psa 127:1). Let the Christian labour at his walls with all diligence, and lay the whole weight of the outcome upon the LORD, who alone makes the fortress stand or lets it fall.

etymology: Hebrew Tirtsah, “delight” or “pleasantness,” a Canaanite royal city that became the early capital of the northern kingdom before Samaria.
biblical_def: Tirzah was a city of beauty and of blood. Its name means delight, and Solomon set it beside Jerusalem as the very figure of loveliness: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners” (Son 6:4). Yet this fair city became the seat of apostate kings. To Tirzah Jeroboam’s wife came in vain to save her dying son: “And Jeroboam’s wife arose, and departed, and came to Tirzah: and when she came to the threshold of the door, the child died” (1Ki 14:17). There Baasha reigned, and there Elah his son after him — “began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah” (1Ki 16:8) — until Zimri murdered him and, besieged, “burnt the king’s house over him with fire, and died” (1Ki 16:18). Omri would soon abandon Tirzah for Samaria. So the delight of the north became a byword for treachery and short-lived crowns. The lesson is stern: outward beauty and a pleasant name cannot cover a throne built on idolatry. The city comely as Jerusalem was not comely in the sight of God, for its kings walked in the sin of Jeroboam. Loveliness without holiness is a whited sepulchre.
webster_summary: The early capital of the northern kingdom (1Ki 16:8), a city whose name means “delight” (Son 6:4) yet became a seat of apostate, blood-stained kings.
webster_full: TIRZAH, a Canaanite royal city, later the first capital of Israel before Omri built Samaria.

corruption_summary: The delightful early capital of the north; the entry recovers that outward beauty and a fair name cannot sanctify a throne built on idolatry.
corruption_paragraphs: Tirzah’s corruption is the ancient confusion of beauty with goodness. A city named delight, comely as Jerusalem, was nonetheless the seat of Jeroboam’s calves and of murdering kings. The eye admired what the heart of God abhorred. The perennial temptation is to reckon a thing holy because it is lovely, or true because it is admired.

The modern form of the error prizes the aesthetic and the appealing above the holy: what pleases the eye and the taste is called good, and beauty is made its own justification. But Tirzah teaches that a fair name and a comely face may crown an idolatrous throne. The Lord looks not on the outward appearance but on the heart (1Sa 16:7). Loveliness severed from obedience is the whited sepulchre; only holiness makes a city truly comely before God.

etymology: Hebrew Teqoa', from a root meaning “to pitch (a tent)” or “to blow (a trumpet),” a town in the wilderness hills of Judah south of Bethlehem.
biblical_def: Tekoa sat on the bleak upland border of the Judean wilderness, a place of shepherds and sycomore fruit. From it Joab fetched an instrument of policy: “And Joab sent to Tekoah, and fetched thence a wise woman” (2Sa 14:2), who by a feigned parable moved David to recall banished Absalom. But Tekoa’s true glory is a herdsman-prophet. “The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa” (Amo 1:1) — no son of the prophets, no court-trained scribe, but a keeper of cattle and dresser of sycomore trees, whom the LORD took as he followed the flock and sent to thunder against the fat cows of Bashan and the ivory beds of Samaria. Rehoboam had also fortified the town: “He built even Bethlehem, and Etam, and Tekoa” (2Ch 11:6). And when the northern storm gathered, Jeremiah cried, “blow the trumpet in Tekoa” (Jer 6:1), a wordplay on its very name. Tekoa teaches that God delights to raise His witnesses from the wilderness and the sheepfold, not from the academy of the proud. The plain herdsman with a word from heaven outweighs a hundred hirelings with credentials and no commission. The LORD chooses the low things, that no flesh should glory in His presence.
webster_summary: A town on the edge of the Judean wilderness south of Bethlehem, home of the wise woman (2Sa 14:2) and of Amos the herdsman-prophet (Amo 1:1).
webster_full: TEKOA, a town in the wilderness hills of Judah, south of Bethlehem.

Fortified by Rehoboam (2Ch 11:6); its name echoes the blown trumpet (Jer 6:1).

corruption_summary: The wilderness town of Amos the herdsman; the entry recovers that God raises His witnesses from the sheepfold, not the academy of the proud.
corruption_paragraphs: Tekoa raises no culture-war quarrel, but it rebukes a persistent conceit: that a true word from God must come credentialed, polished, and academically approved. Amos was a herdsman and a dresser of sycomore trees, taken by the LORD from following the flock. The office was not in his pedigree but in his commission.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereign freedom of God in calling His servants. He chooses the weak and the base and the despised, that no flesh should glory in His presence (1Co 1:27-29). The plain man with a genuine word from heaven outweighs the learned hireling with no commission. Tekoa summons the church to prize the calling of God above the applause of men, and to blow the trumpet faithfully wherever He sends.

etymology: Hebrew Tappuach, “apple” or “apple place,” the name of towns on the border of Ephraim and Manasseh and in the lowland of Judah.
biblical_def: Tappuah, the “apple town,” marks a border. On the great line between the sons of Joseph it stood: “The border went out from Tappuah westward unto the river Kanah” (Jos 16:8), and the boundary between the two tribes ran through its very fields: “Now Manasseh had the land of Tappuah: but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim” (Jos 17:8). Its Canaanite king had already fallen before Joshua: “The king of Tappuah, one” (Jos 12:17). Another Tappuah lay in the lowland of Judah: “And Zanoah, and Engannim, Tappuah, and Enam” (Jos 15:34). The careful drawing of these lines is not tedious record but covenant faithfulness: the LORD who promised the land to Abraham measured it out tribe by tribe and field by field, so that every family had its portion by lot from His hand. Tappuah on the seam between Ephraim and Manasseh testifies that God is a God of order, not confusion, and that the inheritance of His people is no vague hope but a surveyed and given possession. The lines are fallen unto His saints in pleasant places; their heritage is sure because He apportions it.
webster_summary: A border town between Ephraim and Manasseh (Jos 16:8; 17:8), with another in the lowland of Judah (Jos 15:34); a witness to the exact, covenanted apportioning of the inheritance.
webster_full: TAPPUAH, “apple place,” a town on the Ephraim-Manasseh border, and another in the Judean lowland.

The tribal boundary ran through its land (Jos 16:8; 17:8).

A witness to the ordered, lot-given apportioning of Israel’s inheritance.

corruption_summary: A border town of the apple; the entry recovers that God apportions His people’s inheritance by exact and faithful measure, not by chance.
corruption_paragraphs: Tappuah stirs no modern controversy, but the boundary it marks rebukes the assumption that the land-lists of Joshua are dry and dispensable record. Every measured line is the LORD keeping His oath to Abraham, dividing the promise field by field so that no tribe was forgotten and no family left without a portion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is a God of order, and that the inheritance of His people rests upon His faithful apportioning. The lines are fallen unto the saints in pleasant places (Psa 16:6). What looks like tedious geography is the surveyor’s proof of a covenant kept. So too the believer’s eternal inheritance is not a vague hope but a portion measured, sealed, and reserved by the hand of God.

etymology: Hebrew Yanoach, “rest” or “resting place,” the name of a town in Naphtali and (as Janohah) on the border of Ephraim.
biblical_def: Janoah, whose name means “rest,” knew little rest. In the north it lay in the land of Naphtali, and when the Assyrian flood rose it was among the first swept away: “came Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor” (2Ki 15:29), carrying the people captive to Assyria. A town called rest was given no rest, for the covenant curse had come upon a rebellious kingdom. On the border of Ephraim another Janohah stood: “the border went about eastward unto Taanathshiloh, and passed by it on the east to Janohah” (Jos 16:6), and “it went down from Janohah to Ataroth, and to Naarath” (Jos 16:7). The irony of the name preaches a sermon. There is no true rest in a land under judgment, no security in walls when the LORD sends the spoiler for sin. Yet the very longing embedded in the name points beyond itself: the rest that Canaan could not finally give remains for the people of God (Heb 4:9). Janoah of the north fell because the people forsook the Lord of the sabbath; the believer finds his rest not in a town or a border but in Christ, who says, Come unto me, and I will give you rest.
webster_summary: A town of Naphtali (2Ki 15:29) carried captive by Assyria, and a border town of Ephraim (Jos 16:6); its name means “rest,” a rest a land under judgment could not keep.
webster_full: JANOAH (Janohah), “rest,” a town of Naphtali and a border town of Ephraim.
The northern Janoah was taken by Tiglathpileser and its people deported (2Ki 15:29).

A name meaning rest, given to towns that found none under judgment.
A pointer to the true rest that remains for the people of God in Christ.

corruption_summary: A town named “rest” carried into exile; the entry recovers that no land under judgment can give rest, which remains only in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Janoah’s lesson is the emptiness of a promised rest that man seeks apart from God. A town named rest was among the first the Assyrian carried away, for a kingdom sunk in the sin of Jeroboam had forfeited the peace of the covenant. The name mocked the ruin until the ruin taught the name’s true meaning.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true rest is a gift of God in Christ, not a possession of geography or of human striving. Canaan itself was a shadow; the substance is the sabbath-rest that remains for the people of God (Heb 4:9-10). The world offers a hundred counterfeit rests, and every one is carried away in its hour. Janoah bids the weary soul come to Him who alone gives rest to the labouring and heavy laden.

etymology: Hebrew Eleph, likely “the ox” or “a thousand,” a small town in the inheritance of Benjamin near Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Eleph is a town so small that Scripture names it once and passes on: “And Zelah, Eleph, and Jebusi, which is Jerusalem, Gibeath, and Kirjath; fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the children of Benjamin” (Jos 18:28). It appears only in the roll of Benjamin’s allotment, one obscure name among fourteen, its very location now uncertain. Yet it was written in the book of the covenant land. The whole lot fell to Benjamin by the appointment of God: “And the lot of the tribe of the children of Benjamin came up according to their families: and the coast of their lot came forth between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph” (Jos 18:11), among cities that included “Jericho, and Bethhoglah, and the valley of Keziz” (Jos 18:21). Eleph preaches the dignity of the small and the forgotten. The God who counts the hairs of the head and marks the sparrow’s fall did not disdain to record a hamlet whose stones have vanished from the earth. Every name in the inheritance was written because the LORD keeps His promises down to the least detail. So the humblest saint, unknown to the world, is named and numbered in the Lamb’s book of life. The lines are fallen unto him in pleasant places; his heritage is sure.
webster_summary: A small, now-unlocated town in the inheritance of Benjamin, named once (Jos 18:28); a witness that God records and keeps even the least and most obscure of His people’s portion.

corruption_paragraphs: Eleph faces no modern redefinition; it is barely known at all. Yet its single mention rebukes the worldly reckoning that measures worth by fame and size. A town whose very site is lost was written into the covenant record because God keeps His promises down to the least detail.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the tender particularity of God’s care. He numbers the sparrows and the hairs of the head, and He did not disdain to name a vanished hamlet in the inheritance of Benjamin. The humblest and most obscure believer is written in the Lamb’s book of life, named and kept by the same faithfulness. Eleph assures the forgotten that they are not forgotten of God.

etymology: Hebrew Qenath, “possession,” a city in the region of Bashan or Gilead east of Jordan, renamed Nobah by its captor.
biblical_def: Kenath was a strong city of the east, and its story is a small parable of pride. “And Nobah went and took Kenath, and the villages thereof, and called it Nobah, after his own name” (Num 32:42). The conqueror could not rest until the possession he seized also bore his name; the man overwrote the city’s title with his own vanity. Yet the LORD did not honour the presumption, for Scripture and history alike kept calling the place Kenath. Later the men of Geshur and Aram wrested it away: “And he took Geshur, and Aram, with the towns of Jair, from them, with Kenath, and the towns thereof, even threescore cities” (1Ch 2:23). The region belonged to the sons of Machir, in the land the LORD had given: “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine” (Psa 60:7), saith the God who owns the east and the west. Nobah renamed a city; God owns the world. Here is the folly of every empire and every man who stamps his name upon what he cannot keep, as though a title deed of vanity could bind what belongs to the Almighty. Jair took the small towns and called them after himself (Num 32:41); Nobah did the same; and the names have faded while the word of God endures. The meek, not the self-namers, inherit the earth.
webster_summary: A city of Bashan or Gilead (Num 32:42) that its captor Nobah vainly renamed after himself; a parable of the pride that stamps its name on what it cannot keep.
webster_full: KENATH, a fortified city east of Jordan, in the region of Bashan or Gilead.

A parable of the vanity that overwrites God’s world with its own name.

corruption_summary: A city renamed by its captor after himself; the entry recovers that God owns the earth, and the self-namer cannot keep what he seizes.
corruption_paragraphs: Kenath’s corruption is the ancient itch of self-glory: to seize a possession and brand it with one’s own name, as Nobah did. It is the builder of Babel over again, making a name for himself. The world is full of monuments, towers, and titles by which men labour to immortalize themselves against oblivion.

The modern culture of self-branding and the endless monument to the autonomous self is the same conceit in new dress. But Gilead is God’s and Manasseh is God’s (Psa 60:7); the earth is the LORD’s and the fulness thereof. Nobah’s name faded while the word of God endures, and every self-exalting name will fade the same way. The meek inherit the earth; the self-namers inherit the wind. Let a man seek rather to have his name written in heaven.
roots_summary: Hebrew Qenath, “possession,” a city of the east renamed Nobah by its captor.

etymology: Hebrew Salkah (also Salcah), a city marking the eastern border of Bashan, in the kingdom of Og.
biblical_def: Salchah stood at the far eastern edge of the promised land, the border-marker of Bashan and the kingdom of the giant Og. When Israel measured what the LORD had given east of Jordan, the reckoning reached to Salchah: “All the cities of the plain, and all Gilead, and all Bashan, unto Salchah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan” (Deu 3:10). Og had “reigned in mount Hermon, and in Salcah, and in all Bashan” (Jos 12:5), yet that mighty king, last of the remnant of giants, fell before the God of Israel, and his border towns passed to Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh: “all Bashan unto Salcah” (Jos 13:11). There the children of Gad dwelt: “the children of Gad dwelt over against them, in the land of Bashan unto Salchah” (1Ch 5:11). Salchah teaches that the reach of God’s promise is not vague but bordered, and that the mightiest giant cannot hold his gate against the LORD. Og’s iron bedstead and towering stature were nothing before the arm that gave his cities to shepherds and farmers. The uttermost border-town of a giant’s realm became a quiet possession of the covenant people, a standing witness that no stronghold of the mighty can withstand the word of the Almighty.
webster_summary: The eastern border city of Bashan in Og’s kingdom (Deu 3:10; Jos 12:5); a witness that the mightiest giant cannot hold his gate against the LORD.
webster_full: SALCHAH (Salcah), a city marking the eastern border of Bashan.

A witness that no giant’s stronghold can stand against God.

corruption_summary: The eastern border city of the giant Og’s Bashan; the entry recovers that no stronghold of the mighty can stand against the word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Salchah faces no modern redefinition, but it silences an old boast: that strength and stature and iron can secure a man against every foe. Og was a giant, his bedstead of iron a marvel, his cities set on the high plateau of Bashan. Yet his gate at Salchah could not hold against the LORD, and his realm was parceled out to herdsmen.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereign might of God over every human power. The world still trusts in the giant, the fortress, and the reach of its arm; but the LORD gives the strong cities of the mighty into the hands of the weak He has chosen. Salchah, the uttermost border of a giant’s kingdom, became a quiet possession of the covenant people. No stronghold, however towering, can withstand the word of the Almighty.

etymology: Hebrew Ether, likely “abundance” or “entreaty,” a town in the lowland of Judah later reckoned to Simeon.
biblical_def: Ether belonged to the shared inheritance of Judah and Simeon, a town of the lowland named among the cities of the tribe of Judah — “Libnah, and Ether, and Ashan” (Jos 15:42) — and then again among the towns given within Judah to Simeon: “Ain, Remmon, and Ether, and Ashan; four cities and their villages” (Jos 19:7). Simeon’s peculiar portion carried a prophecy from Jacob’s deathbed, that this tribe would be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel; and so Simeon received no separate territory but a cluster of towns like Ether folded inside the larger land of Judah. The name may signify abundance or entreaty. Ether is otherwise silent in the record, one of the many small towns that fill the allotment lists. But its double mention testifies to the exactness of God’s dividing and to the mercy that gave scattered Simeon a place after all. Even the tribe under a word of judgment was not cast off; it dwelt among its brethren, sharing Judah’s abundance. Ether preaches that God’s discipline is not His rejection, and that the tribe humbled by prophecy still received bread and a portion in the land of promise. The Lord chastens whom He loves, and He gives His erring children a home.
webster_summary: A lowland town of Judah assigned within Judah to Simeon (Jos 15:42; 19:7); a witness that the scattered tribe under Jacob’s word of discipline still received a portion of mercy.

A witness that disciplined Simeon still received a place of mercy.

corruption_summary: A shared town of Judah and Simeon; the entry recovers that God’s discipline is not rejection, and the chastened still receive a portion of mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: Ether raises no modern quarrel, yet its assignment to Simeon rebukes a common misreading of God’s discipline as His abandonment. Simeon had a word of scattering upon it from Jacob, and received no separate land; but it was not cast out. It dwelt in towns like Ether, folded within the abundance of Judah.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Lord chastens whom He loves, and His correction is fatherly, not final. Simeon divided in Israel still ate Judah’s bread and held Judah’s towns. The believer under the rod must not read the discipline as disinheritance; the lines still fall in pleasant places (Psa 16:6). Ether, a small town of the scattered tribe, testifies that God gives even His erring children a home.

etymology: Hebrew 'Aro'er, likely “ruins” or “bare place,” a city on the northern brink of the river Arnon, the border-marker of the Amorite kingdom.
biblical_def: Aroer perched on the very brink of the Arnon gorge, the frontier post of the trans-Jordan. When Israel overthrew Sihon, the conquest began here: “From Aroer, which is by the brink of the river of Arnon—there was not one city too strong for us: the LORD our God delivered all unto us” (Deu 2:36). Sihon had “ruled from Aroer, which is upon the bank of the river Arnon” (Jos 12:2), and after him the town became a boundary-stone of Israel’s eastern inheritance, where David’s census-takers “pitched in Aroer” (2Sa 24:5). Centuries later, when judgment swept Moab, Aroer stood again as a lookout on the road of flight: “O inhabitant of Aroer, stand by the way, and espy; ask him that fleeth” (Jer 48:19). A city named “ruins” watched empires rise and fall along its cliff. Aroer proclaims that no border is too strong when the LORD wills to give it, and none too secure when He wills to overthrow it. The same word that says “not one city too strong for us” also sets the watcher of Aroer to count the refugees of a fallen kingdom. Man builds his fortress on the edge of the chasm; God alone decides whether it stands as a gate of victory or a milestone of ruin.
webster_summary: A city on the brink of the Arnon (Deu 2:36), border of the Amorite realm and later of Israel; a frontier-stone that watched empires rise and fall by the will of God.

corruption_summary: A frontier city on the Arnon; the entry recovers that no border is too strong to be given, nor too secure to be overthrown, when the LORD wills.
corruption_paragraphs: Aroer raises no modern controversy, but its cliff-top vigil rebukes the confidence of the fortified. Men set their strongest cities on the edge of the chasm and call them impregnable; yet at Aroer there was not one city too strong for the LORD to give, and the same Aroer became a watch-post over Moab’s ruin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s absolute sway over the rise and fall of powers. The nations trust their frontiers and their arms, but the God of Israel delivers the strong city into the hands He chooses and sends the watcher to count the refugees of the proud. Aroer preaches that history is not the story of the strong prevailing, but of the Almighty ruling; and the wise man builds his hope not on the cliff’s edge but on the Rock.
